title: Business applications and employer-firm formation are different local economic stages
source_unit: NBER Working Paper 34881; linked administrative microdata tracking the universe of U.S. business applications and transitions into employer firms
geography: United States counties and local areas; business applications and employer-firm transitions

observations.period: U.S. business applications and employer transitions; paper issued February 2026

stage_definition.value: business entry has distinct pursuit and implementation stages: application followed by transition into an employer firm

high_startup_locations.value: high-startup locations are characterized by high application intensity

low_startup_locations.value: low-startup locations exhibit low transition rates from applications into employer firms

local_dynamics.value: application and transition margins associate differently with local conditions

observations.method: The authors link administrative records for the universe of U.S. business applications to later employer-firm outcomes and model entry as pursuit of an idea followed by implementation, comparing how both stages vary with local conditions.
observations.uncertainty: The public abstract does not follow each applicant's household resources, financing, lease, permit, customers, service quality, local belonging, or later closure reason. A transition into an employer firm is not the same as durable survival, good jobs, local service, or community capacity.
observations.subgroup: U.S. local areas with different application intensity and application-to-employer transition rates; industry, urbanity, credit, labor supply, rent, infrastructure, public demand, and customer access can differ across places.
observations.counterinterpretation: High applications may reflect many ideas, necessity entry, or administrative composition rather than strong local opportunity. Low transition may reflect deliberate non-employer activity, not failed entrepreneurship. Employer formation can create jobs while displacing another firm or providing low-quality work; the study does not settle those outcomes.

related_sources.claim: NBER DOI record for Working Paper 34881

boundary: This record adds a local conversion finding: an application is pursuit, while an employer firm is implementation. It does not establish durable survival, job quality, local service, customer benefit, household welfare, belonging, or political participation.
